nature-eco-624.q: Name some kinds of natural disturbance an ecosystem can face.
nature-eco-624.a: Fires, floods, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions; they range from one falling tree to a mass extinction.

nature-eco-640.q: What does the word hysteresis mean, and who coined it?
nature-eco-640.a: Sir James Alfred Ewing coined it in 1881, from a Greek word meaning 'lagging behind'.

nature-eco-597.q: What could happen if humanity crosses the planetary boundaries?
nature-eco-597.a: The Earth system could be pushed out of the stable Holocene period in which human society developed.

nature-eco-598.q: What is the climate boundary for carbon dioxide in the air, and where are we now?
nature-eco-598.a: The boundary is 350 ppm; the current level is 423 ppm, against 280 ppm before industry.

nature-eco-608.q: Which tipping elements are likely to tip at 1.5 °C of warming?
nature-eco-608.a: Collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets, die-off of tropical coral reefs and sudden thaw of northern permafrost.

nature-eco-643.q: What did William R. Catton Jr.'s 1980 book Overshoot blame?

nature-eco-602.q: What does William Schlesinger warn about managing an ecosystem up to a threshold?
nature-eco-602.a: It lets slow, spread-out damage carry on almost indefinitely.

nature-eco-626.q: How does a mountain pine beetle outbreak change a western North American forest?
nature-eco-626.a: It kills old pines, opening gaps where other trees do well until the pines grow back.

nature-eco-612.q: Around what level of warming might this threshold lie?
nature-eco-612.a: Researchers proposed about 2 °C above pre-industrial levels.

nature-eco-631.q: Who argued that diverse communities are more stable, and who refuted it?
nature-eco-631.a: Charles Elton argued it in 1958; Robert May later refuted the idea that diversity begets stability.

nature-eco-641.q: How can a recession leave lasting unemployment?
nature-eco-641.a: Jobless workers may lose skills or motivation and stay out of work even during the recovery.

nature-eco-650.q: What are the four phases of the adaptive cycle?
nature-eco-650.a: A slow move from exploitation (r) to conservation (K), then a fast release (Omega) and reorganisation (alpha) before exploitation again.

nature-eco-618.q: How do state variables differ from parameters?
nature-eco-618.a: State variables, like population densities, respond quickly to feedbacks; parameters respond slowly or not at all.

nature-eco-655.q: What is panarchy in resilience theory?
nature-eco-655.a: How much one level of an ecosystem's hierarchy is influenced by other levels; C.S. Holling developed the idea.

nature-eco-410.q: Why can mangroves live where most plants die?
nature-eco-410.a: Special adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and get rid of salt.

nature-eco-563.q: Why are rainforest soils often poor?
nature-eco-563.a: Heavy rain washes out nutrients, and most nutrients sit near the surface because leaves and organisms rot quickly.

nature-eco-565.q: What are the three types of tundra?

nature-eco-449.q: What is the cheapest, least intrusive way to restore a wetland?
nature-eco-449.a: Stop the disturbance and leave the wetland to recover by natural succession.

nature-es-082.q: How do mangroves build up the land they grow on?
nature-es-082.a: By slowing incoming tides, they make sediment settle out.

nature-eco-530.a: They are transition zones where river and sea environments overlap.

nature-eco-470.q: Where is most grassland carbon stored?
nature-eco-470.a: In the soil, which holds about 81% of all carbon in grassland ecosystems.

nature-eco-478.q: Why does draining a peatland release greenhouse gases?
nature-eco-478.a: Drainage lets oxygen into the peat, so it decomposes and gives off carbon dioxide and methane.

nature-eco-513.q: Why do caribou move into boreal areas in winter?

nature-eco-561.q: How does this forest biome's share of world forest compare with the boreal forest's?
nature-eco-561.a: It is second largest with 25%, behind the boreal forest's roughly 33%.

nature-eco-417.q: What share of land-dwelling organisms do forests host?

nature-eco-535.q: How do algal blooms eventually affect fish?
nature-eco-535.a: They can briefly boost fish numbers, but continued loss of oxygen then makes fish populations fall.

nature-eco-453.q: How much of the ocean do coral reefs cover, and how many marine species live there?
nature-eco-453.a: Less than 0.1% of the ocean, yet at least 25% of all marine species.

nature-eco-422.q: How do kelp forests and coral reefs compare in area and productivity?
nature-eco-422.a: They cover only 0.1% of Earth's surface but account for 0.9% of global primary productivity.

nature-eco-460.q: Do marine protected areas always work?
nature-eco-460.a: Their effectiveness is debated: some sites showed no difference from unprotected areas, and some caused local conflict.

nature-eco-427.q: How can overfishing destroy a kelp forest?
nature-eco-427.a: Removing predators lets the forest collapse into an urchin barren.

nature-eco-459.a: Rising sea temperatures from greenhouse gas emissions.

nature-eco-462.q: Why are floodplain soils often very fertile?

nature-eco-472.q: Why was a map of land for forest restoration criticised?
nature-eco-472.a: It included 900 million hectares of grasslands among its 2 billion hectares.

nature-eco-484.q: What does a strip of undisturbed land along a stream do during logging?
nature-eco-484.a: It gives shade, leaf litter and wood, and holds back soil eroded from the logged area.

nature-eco-466.q: Where does much of the phosphorus in fresh water come from?
nature-eco-466.a: Wastewater treatment plants and farm runoff.

nature-eco-435.q: How has the view of salt marshes changed?
nature-eco-435.a: Once seen as wasteland, they are now known as among the most productive habitats on Earth, rivalling tropical rainforests.

nature-eco-560.a: The average time for fires to burn an area equal to the whole ecosystem.

nature-eco-426.q: How much carbon dioxide do seaweeds such as kelp take up each year?

nature-eco-489.q: How do seagrass leaves shape the seafloor?
nature-eco-489.a: They slow currents so sediment settles and builds up the bottom; without them, currents carry it away.

nature-eco-542.q: What keeps mangroves in warm climates?

nature-eco-543.q: After about how long does a mangrove forest stop adding biomass?
nature-eco-543.a: About 20–30 years; carbon fixed after that must be stored in sediment, exported or lost to the air.

nature-eco-527.a: In Western Asia and South America.

nature-eco-529.q: What makes dryland restoration more successful, according to case studies?
nature-eco-529.a: Involving indigenous knowledge and local communities.

nature-eco-557.q: What feeds the food web in small, shaded headwater streams?

nature-eco-519.q: What makes these ecosystems unusual in their energy source?
nature-eco-519.a: They are among the few that do not depend on sunlight.

nature-eco-496.q: What mainly decides how much methane a wetland releases?
nature-eco-496.a: How much methane made by methanogens escapes before methanotrophs break it down.

nature-eco-439.q: What happens when cities replace forests, wetlands and grasslands?
nature-eco-439.a: Losing green space lowers air and water quality, health and biodiversity.

nature-es-005.q: What did Plato understand about forests around 400 BC?
nature-es-005.a: That cutting them down could cause soil erosion and dry up springs.

nature-es-002.q: Give examples of services that nature provides.
nature-es-002.a: Purifying air and water, breaking down wastes, pollinating crops, recharging groundwater and reducing greenhouse gases.

nature-es-084.q: How do energy and nutrients move differently through an ecosystem?
nature-es-084.a: Energy flows one way and is not reused, while mineral nutrients move in cycles.
